Forecasters attempting to predict infectious disease outbreaks have met with varying success.
This variation might come from many contributing factors.
One such set of varying factors is the predictive ability of different forecasting methods.
Another set of varying factors is the predictive difficulty of different forecast targets.
With increasing numbers of both forecasters and forecast targets, we have more potential to learn about which factors can be modified to improve forecast performance, and to set appropriate expectations for performance between different forecast settings.
This requires careful accounting among the many factors contributing to performance.
Here, we suggest one approach to this using a joint modelling framework, and apply this to illustrate varying performance of forecasts of Covid-19 in Europe.

Some of the variation in performance can be attributed to differences between infectious disease target estimands.
We see better predictive performance with stable epidemic dynamics [@bracher2022] in larger populations [@lopez2024], and when the target is observed with timely, accurate surveillance [@reich2019] [@holcomb2023], or has informative leading indicators [@delvalle2018].
Meanwhile, performance is consistently better at shorter than longer horizons [@cramer2022], possibly based on the disease-specific serial interval that links disease to observation [@sherratt2023], prompting suggestions that there are inherent limits to the predictability of infectious diseases based on the complexity of the disease-surveillance-response system [@scarpino2019].
This variability makes it difficult to make fair comparisons across multiple forecast targets.

At the same time, variation in performance between forecasters arises from individual differences in the forecast estimation process: the structural approach and implementation choices made in developing a forecasting model.
Forecasters may use many methods, ranging from purely data-driven statistical methods, to mechanistic models that embed explicit hypotheses about biological or epidemiological drivers of transmission.
Different structural approaches may be better suited to different purposes, for example scenario projection, policy analysis, or real-time nowcasting.
This choice demands a trade-off among complementary strengths and weaknesses of different methods [@woolhouse2011; @dattner2018; @funk2020], any of which may impact predictive accuracy.
Previous work has compared predictive performance between these approaches, and shown little evidence for substantial differences [@carlson2018; @viboud2018; @reich2019].

This creates two sets of contributing factors to any single instance of realised performance @fig-processes.
Identifying these influences is important in order to fairly evaluate between different forecasters, and to set appropriate expectations for performance between different forecast settings.

```{r}

#|   Factors that generate the forecast (e.g. model specification), and factors that generate the target (e.g. epidemic dynamics) may each contribute to realised predictive performance.

digraph processes {
  graph [rankdir = TB, fontname = "inherit", bgcolor = "white"]

  subgraph cluster_FG {
    label = "Forecast-generating process"; color = "black"; fontcolor = "black"

  }

  T [label = "Target"]
  P [label = "Predictive performance"]

}
')
```

To evaluate the contribution of different factors to predictive performance, we need a comparable sample of many independent forecasting models across many forecast targets [@pollett2020; @reich2022].
This comparability is achieved in participatory forecast challenges, which collate multiple forecasters' predictions for pre-specified targets in a standardised format [@reich2022].
This offers the opportunity for consistent evaluation between models, with the potential to explicitly compare the value of different modelling approaches @reich2022.

However, such analysis is challenging, as it is prone to selection bias and confounding when evaluating among forecasters with differential participation across forecast targets.
Aggregated comparisons may conflate differences in the predictive performance of each modelling approach, with differences in forecast target difficulty.

Evaluators facing this challenge have borrowed, mostly implicitly, from the tools offered by traditional observational research to control bias (@tbl-approaches).
Epidemiology distinguishes those applied when a study is designed, such as restriction and matching, from those applied to data already collected, such as stratification, standardisation and regression adjustment [@mcnamee2005; @kahlert2017].
In forecast evaluation this distinction largely collapses, because the evaluator is almost always working with forecasts already submitted, and applies such tools retrospectively.

One source of bias is the exception: differential participation could be removed at the point of collection, by a protocol requiring every model to forecast every target, but this is available to hub organisers rather than to anyone evaluating afterwards.
We therefore restrict @tbl-approaches to tools available retrospectively, and order them by the stage of the analysis at which each acts: what enters the sample, how the exposure and the outcome are measured, how units are compared, and how the estimate is computed.
Within the elements governing how units are compared, from matching through to regression adjustment, the sequence is also one of increasing formality, in the sense that each uses clearer and stronger assumptions to account for variation.
This ordering does not extend to the whole table: complete ascertainment and unbiased classification of the exposure are prerequisites to any comparison rather than weaker forms of it.
Each of these tools may usefully simplify some aspect of the problem.
However, evaluators facing large, open forecasting challenges must handle a high degree of variation across both many forecast targets and many forecasting models simultaneously.
The noisiness of these mixed signals means that the simpler strategies may not be sufficient to isolate a single component of forecast performance and trace its effect.

| Study design element | In observational research | In forecast evaluation | Threat addressed | Limitation |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| Inclusion criteria | Exclude units with particular covariate values so the covariate cannot vary | Exclude targets whose observed data were revised after forecasts were made [@sherratt2023]; or exclude models below a submission threshold | Confounding, selection | Loses power; narrows the population the estimate applies to |
| Measurement of exposure | Classify exposure without sight of the outcome, and report agreement between assessors | Classify the model characteristic under comparison from submitted metadata, with the classifier blind to scores | Information | Metadata are self-reported and thin; misclassification remains, and attenuates effects toward the null |
| Scale of outcome | Express the outcome so it does not depend on a nuisance quantity: rates rather than counts, or ratios rather than differences | Score forecasts per 100,000 population, and on the log scale so the score reflects relative rather than absolute error [@bosse2022; @bosse2023] | Confounding by population size and by incidence magnitude | Removes the dependence by redefining what is measured, not by adjusting for it; the quantity compared is no longer error on the natural scale |
| Unadjusted comparison | Report the crude association between exposure and outcome, with no control | Rank models, or compare mean scores between structures, over all forecasts as submitted | None | Conflates the method used with the difficulty of the targets each model chose to forecast |
| Matching on covariates | Pair exposed and unexposed units on covariate values | Compare forecasters only on targets both submitted for [@bracher2021] | Confounding | Sparse overlap; the estimate holds only for the matched set |
| Stratification | Estimate the association within levels of a covariate, then pool | Report scores by horizon, location, or epidemic phase [@reich2019; @cramer2022] | Confounding | Cells sparse and uneven with several interacting factors; continuous covariates need arbitrary binning |
| Indirect standardisation | Compare observed events against those expected under a reference rate, as in a standardised mortality ratio | Relative skill against a naive baseline model available for all targets [@bracher2021] | Confounding by target difficulty | Interpretable only against the chosen reference, which materially changes rankings [@stapper] |
| Regression adjustment | Enter covariates in a model; read the partial association | Estimate the partial effect of model structure adjusting for outcome, incidence, trend, variant, country, horizon, and model | Confounding, clustering | Specification-dependent; the estimand is not formally defined |
| Quantitative bias analysis | Derive a minimal sufficient adjustment set from a directed acyclic graph [@hernan2020]; bound unmeasured confounding with an E-value [@vanderweele2017] | Not yet applied in forecast evaluation | Residual confounding | Requires metadata and sample size that current hubs do not provide |

: Approaches to controlling bias in comparative forecast evaluation, with analogous tools from observational study design. Rows follow the sequence of analysis: what enters the sample, measurement of exposure and outcome, comparison across units of observation, and estimation. {#tbl-approaches}

For example, we may wish to assess the performance of different model designs used by a set of independent forecasters participating in any number of different forecast targets.
When assessing across multiple forecast targets, we would need to separate out the model structure from the adaptability of different model structures to produce predictions across the different forecast targets.
Faced with multiple forecasting targets, a forecaster might produce forecasts for any given target given only updated data, as is typical of statistical time-series and many semi-mechanistic models.
An alternative strategy is to structure a model to mechanistically capture the data-generating processes of a specific forecast target, for example emphasising particular epidemic dynamics or exploiting local data sources.
This suggests the hypothesis that design strategy has a separate influence on predictive performance, confounding an estimate of the effect of model structure alone on predictive performance.

Here, we develop a framework to identify the partial effect of model structure on predictive performance, while jointly adjusting for factors contributing to forecast target difficulty.
We use proper scoring rules to evaluate short-term forecasts of COVID-19 across Europe.
We analyse performance by model structure, using a generalised additive mixed model to also account for variation in the target epidemiological outcome, trend and level of incident outcomes, dominant variant phase, country, forecast horizon, and random error of each individual model.
Rather than stratifying scores across these sparse, interacting subgroups, our hierarchical approach pools information across sparsely populated groups through partial shrinkage of the random effects, and represents continuous sources of difficulty such as incidence as smooth functions.
We include a directed acyclic graph in the Supplement to represent the structure of our assumptions, but note that our work is exploratory rather than formally causal.
We find that, despite superficial differences between model structures, most of the variation in observed performance can be explained by factors associated with the forecast target rather than the forecasting method.
We conclude by noting the increasing breadth and application of infectious disease forecasting efforts, and call for a wider range of evaluative study designs able to accurately and robustly capture their value.
